summary: Defines a QUOTA extension to IMAP that lets administrative limits on resource use, such as mailbox storage, be managed through the protocol. It remains backward compatible with RFC 2087 where possible and obsoletes it.

eli5.summary: It lets a mail program see and set how much space each mailbox may use.

questions: how to check mailbox quota over imap
what is the imap quota extension
what does overquota mean in imap
subtitle: How an IMAP client asks a mail server how much space it has used, and what the limit is.

tldr.problem: The older IMAP quota extension saw little client deployment because resource names were implementation dependent, so clients could not tell which resources were supported or which mailboxes shared a quota.
tldr.mechanism: The extension defines commands to read and set limits on named quota roots, responses that report usage and limit pairs, precisely defined resource types, and an IANA registry for new types.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9208 obsoletes RFC 2087 while trying to stay backwards compatible, and works with both IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2.

today: RFC 9208 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2022. It obsoletes RFC 2087 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 9208 defines extensions to the Internet Message Access Protocol (RFC 3501, RFC 9051) for querying and manipulating administrative quotas: limits on resource usage. It works with both IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2. Quotas can restrict clients for administrative reasons, but can also just tell clients about system limits and current usage.

The older extension, RFC 2087, was deployed in servers but saw little client deployment. Resource meanings were implementation dependent, so a client could not tell which resources were supported, nor which mailboxes were in a given quota root, without prior knowledge of the server.

Capabilities signal what a server supports. The plain QUOTA capability denotes an RFC 2087 server, and clients MUST NOT rely on the new responses unless a capability beginning with QUOTA= is present. A compliant server MUST return at least one QUOTA=RES- capability, and a server that implements SETQUOTA MUST also return QUOTASET.
sections.eli5: Older mail servers could keep a limit on your space, but mail programs could not really understand it. This update makes the rules clear so programs can show you how full you are.

sections.title: Resources and Quota Roots
sections.content:
A resource has a name and a definition. The name is an IMAP atom and MUST be registered with IANA. Supported resources MUST be advertised as capabilities by prefixing the name with QUOTA=RES-. A server need not support every advertised resource on every quota root.

Usage MUST be represented as a 63-bit unsigned integer, where 0 means the resource is exhausted. Limits are also integers, and 0 means any usage is prohibited. Limits may be hard or soft. Because usage does not necessarily represent proportional use, clients MUST NOT compare an available resource between two separate quota roots.

Limits can apply across several mailboxes, so the RFC introduces the quota root. Each mailbox has zero or more implementation-defined named quota roots, and all mailboxes sharing a quota root share its limits. Quota root names are astrings that need not be mailbox names, and clients SHOULD treat them as opaque. A client MUST be prepared for SETQUOTA to fail if a limit cannot be set, and a server may round a limit if the underlying system requires it.
sections.eli5: A quota root is like one shared piggy bank for a group of folders. All the folders in the group draw from the same limit, and the server decides which folders share which bank.

sections.title: Commands, Responses and OVERQUOTA
sections.content:
Three commands manipulate quotas:

  • GETQUOTA takes a quota root name and returns its usage and limits in an untagged QUOTA response.
  • GETQUOTAROOT takes a mailbox name and returns an untagged QUOTAROOT response listing its quota roots, plus a QUOTA response for each. The mailbox need not exist, which helps a client learn which root would apply to a mailbox about to be created.
  • SETQUOTA takes a quota root and a list of limits. It requires the QUOTASET capability. Previous limits are discarded, even for resources not listed in the command.

A QUOTA response lists the quota root name followed by triplets of resource name, current usage and limit. Resources not named are not limited, so an empty list means no administrative limits. For example, QUOTA "" (STORAGE 10 512) reports usage 10 against a limit of 512.

Two new STATUS data items, DELETED and DELETED-STORAGE, let a client estimate what an EXPUNGE would free. The server SHOULD return the exact storage value, but MAY return the sum of the RFC822.SIZE of the messages with the \Deleted flag if exact calculation would take too long.

The OVERQUOTA response code SHOULD be returned in the tagged NO response to an APPEND, COPY or MOVE that would put the target mailbox over any quota limit. It MAY also appear in an untagged NO response when a mailbox exceeds a soft quota, for example after delivery by another connection.
sections.eli5: You can ask "how full is this shelf?", "which shelves share a limit with this folder?", or (if you are allowed) "change the limit". If you try to add something that will not fit, the server says you are over quota.

sections.title: The Four Resource Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines four resource types, each advertised as QUOTA=RES- plus the name:

  • STORAGE: a physical space estimate in units of 1024 octets. It MAY differ from the sum of message sizes, since an implementation may count metadata or compress. Clients MUST NOT use it for anything beyond information, for example they must not refuse an APPEND because of it, though they MAY warn. Servers supporting it MUST support DELETED-STORAGE.
  • MESSAGE: the number of messages in the governed mailboxes. This MUST be an exact number. Servers supporting it MUST support the DELETED status item.
  • MAILBOX: the number of mailboxes governed by the quota root, also exact.
  • ANNOTATION-STORAGE: the maximum size of all annotations (RFC 5257), in units of 1024 octets, on messages in the governed mailboxes.

For the counted types, clients MUST NOT assume a change in usage means a change in what they can see, because the quota root may include mailboxes the client cannot access.
sections.eli5: The server can count a few different things: how much space is used, how many messages there are, how many folders there are, and how much room notes attached to messages take up.

sections.title: Access Rights and IANA Registry
sections.content:
When the IMAP ACL extension (RFC 4314) is also implemented, the RFC lists the rights needed: GETQUOTA needs no rights on a mailbox, SETQUOTA needs the a right, and GETQUOTAROOT depends on the resource. A message-count or storage quota needs the r right, since it would reveal information about the mailbox contents, while MAILBOX needs none.

IANA updated the QUOTA capability entry, added the QUOTA= prefix and the QUOTASET capability, and created an "IMAP Quota Resource Types" registry with the policy "Specification Required". The four resource types above are its initial contents. All other capabilities starting with QUOTA= are reserved for future IETF Stream extensions.
sections.eli5: Some people may not be allowed to peek at how many messages are in a folder, so the rules say who can ask what. There is also an official list where new kinds of limits can be added.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must not violate the site's security policy. Other users' resource usage is likely confidential and should not be given to unauthorized people, and no quota information should be disclosed to anonymous users.

On shared resources, such as a quota root over shared mailboxes, a user who can consume the resource, or who may run SETQUOTA with an artificially small value, can affect the others. Computing usage may also load the server heavily, so implementers should consider caching usage or using less precise computations under heavy load.
sections.eli5: How full someone's mailbox is can be private, so only the right people should see it. And someone who can shrink a shared limit could cause trouble for everyone sharing it.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2087
sections.content: RFC 9208 revises RFC 2087. It clarifies terms, adds examples, gives guidance on allowed server behaviour, defines an IANA registry and registers four resource types. Compared with RFC 2087 it defines two more commonly used resource types, adds an optional OVERQUOTA response code and the DELETED and DELETED-STORAGE STATUS items. For extensibility, usage and limits are now 63-bit unsigned integers.
sections.eli5: The new version explains old fuzzy ideas more clearly, adds a way to say "you are over your limit", and lets the numbers be much bigger.
